sm: The House voted to send a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee, which blocks an impeachment vote for now. Congressman Thomas Massie led the push, accusing Hegseth of carrying out unlawful military orders, including war with Iran without congressional approval. Hegseth called it a political stunt and said every operation was lawful. A bipartisan power grid bill advanced in the Senate, and House Republicans chose Jim Jordan as minority leader over Steve Scalise, 106 to 73. Senate Republicans reelected John Thune. In Israel, most Arab-Israeli lawmakers walked out of the Knesset swearing-in, and three men face terrorism charges in New York over Iran-backed plots.

On Washington Wednesday, political scientist Hunter Baker discussed the new balance of power after the election. He said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries should not struggle to hold his coalition together if his margin is large, since the socialist members would not be decisive. Baker said Democrats could seize a practical, moderate opening as Rahm Emanuel urges, but he doubts they will, expecting efforts against the electoral college and many investigations. The hosts raised Kansas Senator-elect Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor, and James Talarico. Baker strongly disagreed that their tone is a good development, saying faithful Christians cannot avoid abortion and human sexuality. He called Talarico a heretic and doubted Hamilton too.

Baker reacted to the Ross Douthat interview of President Trump on 60 Minutes, in which Trump said he could not forgive his enemies before God. Baker called it high drama and said it answers questions about Trump's faith, saying he is a political ally but not a Christian, and that Christians should pray for him. On the Iran war, Baker said war powers remain ill-defined and Congress can withhold money, but he urged members not to play politics with it. In a lightning round, he said Rick Scott likely skipped challenging Thune over 2028 plans, that the lame duck should prioritize judicial nominees, and that a Trump, Xi and Putin meeting would amount to little.

The hosts turned to World Tour on Haiti. Gangs kidnapped four Salvadoran soldiers serving with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force, and President Nayib Bukele sent two thousand more troops to get them back. There are now more Salvadoran soldiers in Haiti than force troops, and some Haitians welcome them. Bukele cut crime sharply in El Salvador but faces accusations of human rights abuses and eroding the rule of law. Analyst Sandra Pellegrini noted concerns about oversight, drone strikes that killed civilians, and Haiti's weak judicial system. One gang leader asked the UN for mediation, which an observer said may show growing pressure. Haiti plans its first elections in a decade.

A brief story noted that New York's transit agency sold old subway seats for nine hundred dollars a pair, and some buyers installed them at home. The hosts then marked Veterans Day, noting seventeen million veterans. Kim Henderson reported on Marine veterans who meet every other Thursday at a Cracker Barrel in Lynchburg, Virginia. Members including Justin Gregory, Terry Jamerson, Larry Johnson, Walt Allen and retired Major General Jason Baum described their service and the lasting bond of the Corps. Baum said you earn the title Marine and keep it for life. They said most members are Christians or hold Christian ethics. They end by standing to sing the Marines' Hymn.

Commentator Maria Baer argued that people change culture at small scale. She described Hannah Erdle, founder of Delay Smartphones, who started by inviting parents to dinner after asking what motivates people to change behavior. Baer said humans are imitators by nature and are shaped by cultural norms, and that Jesus taught by living out his message in community. She said Christians should challenge bad norms, advance good ones, or create better ones in families, schools, churches and offices, calling it redemption by social contagion. The hosts previewed tomorrow's stories on the education freedom tax credit and an interview with journalist Andy Ngo. The episode closed with a reading from Revelation chapter three.
